question: Who came up with the famous five-stage model of dying and grief?
explanation: You'll see this model everywhere in nursing! It was developed by psychiatrist Elisabeth Kubler-Ross from her work with terminally ill patients. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h1)

question: How do patients usually move through the stages of dying?

options.A: Rapidly within the first twenty-four hours of a diagnosis
options.B: Always starting with depression and ending with anger
options.C: Fluidly, often moving back and forth or skipping steps
options.D: Strictly one after the other in a neat timeline

explanation: Grief is never a straight line. Patients often bounce back and forth or skip steps entirely, and that is completely normal! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of denial when a patient first gets bad news?

options.A: Manipulating family members into giving attention
options.B: Proving that the doctors made a mistake
options.C: Acting as a psychological buffer against overwhelming shock
options.D: Speeding up the body's physical healing

explanation: Denial is actually a soft cushion for the mind, protecting the patient from absorbing too much heavy pain all at once. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h2)

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient insists their terminal test results belong to someone else?

options.A: Ignore the statement and change the hospital topic
options.B: Argue with the patient using hard medical facts
options.C: Agree with the patient that a mistake definitely occurred
options.D: Gently listen and avoid forcing immediate acceptance

explanation: Confronting denial too aggressively can cause extreme distress, so nurses should support the patient while remaining truthful. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which question is a patient in the anger stage most likely to ask?

options.A: How much will this treatment cost?
options.B: When will my test results arrive?
options.D: Why is this happening to me?

explanation: Anger comes from deep hurt and the feeling of unfairness, making patients ask 'Why me?' [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h3)

question: A hospitalized patient snaps angrily at a nurse, complaining that the room is too loud and care is terrible. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Report the patient to the attending physician for verbal abuse
options.B: Argue back to set firm boundaries on respectful communication
options.C: Understand the frustration is a normal part of grief and remain calm
options.D: Leave the room immediately and refuse to return that shift

explanation: Taking anger personally interferes with care; recognizing it as a stage of grief helps maintain a therapeutic relationship. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the main sign of the bargaining stage?

options.A: Directing intense rage at doctors and family members
options.B: Completely accepting the diagnosis without any sorrow
options.C: Isolating oneself from all hospital staff and visitors
options.D: Attempting to negotiate for more time or less pain

explanation: In this stage, patients try to make a 'deal'—often with God or fate—to buy a little more time. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why do patients bargain when facing a terminal illness?

options.A: To regain a temporary sense of control over their fate
options.B: To prove to family members that treatment is working
options.C: To punish medical staff for poor communication
options.D: To manipulate insurance companies into paying bills

explanation: Bargaining is a psychological attempt to grab back some control when everything feels completely out of hand. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h4)

question: What type of depression involves mourning the upcoming loss of life and loved ones?
explanation: This stage is all about deep sadness for what is being left behind, quietly preparing the heart for the end. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h5)

question: How should a nurse approach a terminally ill patient experiencing deep sadness in the depression stage?

options.A: Request an immediate psychiatric consult for clinical antidepressants
options.B: Distract the patient with busy hospital activities and television
options.C: Encourage the patient to cheer up and focus on positive thoughts
options.D: Provide a quiet, supportive presence and allow expression of grief

explanation: Sadness at this stage is a normal reaction, so offering a comforting presence is more helpful than trying to force artificial cheer. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h5)

question: What emotional state best describes the acceptance stage?

options.A: Intense bargaining for extra time with family
options.B: Extreme anger and hostility toward medical providers
options.C: Quiet peace and realistic acknowledgment of mortality
options.D: Joyful celebration of a long life well lived

explanation: Acceptance is marked by a calm, albeit often tired, readiness for the end of life rather than happiness. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h6)

question: What behavior might you notice in a patient who has reached acceptance?

options.A: Conserving energy and withdrawing into quiet reflection
options.B: Arguing with family over small things
options.D: Denying that they have any symptoms at all

explanation: As energy fades, patients in acceptance often quiet down, letting go of worldly fuss to rest in peace. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the biggest flaw in relying too strictly on the Kubler-Ross stages?

options.A: Grief is not a rigid, universal checklist
options.B: It was proven false by lab blood tests
options.C: Patients never experience anger or depression
options.D: It only works for children with cancer

explanation: Every patient handles grief differently. Treating these stages like strict rules can make us miss the person right in front of us. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a good reason to be careful with the Kubler-Ross model?

options.A: It guarantees every patient will have a completely painless death
options.B: Treating the stages as strict rules can hurt individualized care
options.C: It might miss cultural differences in how people grieve
options.D: Patients often skip or repeat stages

explanation: Spot on! The model maps out emotions—it has nothing to do with curing physical pain or guaranteeing a pain-free passing. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the main goal of nursing care for a dying patient?

options.A: Forcing the patient through all five stages of grief
options.B: Maximizing comfort, dignity, and holistic support
options.C: Finding a miracle cure for the disease
options.D: Restricting visitors to keep the room quiet

explanation: At the end of life, our main duty as nurses is palliative care: keeping them comfortable, pain-free, and deeply respected. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h8)

question: A dying patient says they are scared to die alone while family steps out. What should you do?

options.A: Tell them not to worry because family will be back tomorrow
options.B: Sit with them and offer a reassuring, calming presence
options.C: Run out to find the doctor right away
options.D: Tell them to think about happier times

explanation: Sometimes your physical presence is the best medicine. Just staying by their side chases away that terrifying loneliness. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T3#GNS221_U4_T3_h8)
